overview: Tonga's modern kingdom combines a continuing monarchy and parliamentary institutions with vigorous traditions of textile work, poetry, language and community exchange. Surviving barkcloth can record particular events and reveal how makers worked. Political changes in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries reshaped government without ending Tongan cultural life.

periods.title: Constitutional institutions
periods.summary: Parliament opened in 1875 during the creation of Tonga's constitutional system. Ministers, nobles and elected representatives participated, but their roles and powers differed from those of a present-day parliament.

periods.title: A protected kingdom
periods.summary: A treaty with Britain in 1900 established protected-state status. Tonga retained its monarchy and was not administered as a colony on Fiji's model, although British intervention constrained its freedom.

periods.title: After the protectorate
periods.summary: Tonga withdrew from the British protectorate and joined the Commonwealth in 1970. The kingdom continues, with cultural relationships extending to communities overseas.

items.text: A 1940s ngatu hingoa at Te Papa depicts a Spitfire seen from below. It commemorates Tongan support for the Allied war effort. Its makers are unnamed in the surviving collection history, so the detailed design should not be assigned to an invented individual artist.

Conservation examination of that cloth identified two layers of beaten mulberry bark, joined unevenly. The proposed starch adhesive and plant dyes remain qualified identifications. Damage, joins and repairs allow the cloth to be studied as a made object as well as an image.

Another large ngatu was made for Elizabeth II's visit in 1953 and later placed beneath Queen Salote's coffin on her return to Tonga in 1965. Its changing ceremonial use gives one textile a history spanning celebration and mourning.

In a koka'anga work party, women join sheets of beaten inner bark in overlapping layers. They rub dye over cloth laid above kupesi pattern boards, bringing the designs through the surface, then add details by hand. The technique combines repeated patterns with individual decisions.

Lines and numbers at the cloth's border mark langanga, units used to measure its growing length. Te Papa explains that the unit varies with the equipment and the maker. The markings record practical production knowledge, rather than a universal fixed metric.

Ngatu circulate as gifts at weddings, funerals and other gatherings. Exchanges with makers of pandanus mats connect communities with different plant resources. Cloth therefore participates in relationships as well as furnishing and dress.

The first parliament opened on 16 September 1875 to discuss the new constitution. Its members included ministers, nobles and elected representatives. This opening date records an institutional event; it is not the day Tongan people or their islands began to have a history.

Charles St Julian sent George Tupou I a copy of Hawaii's 1852 constitution. Tonga's parliamentary history identifies it as an influence on the new constitutional text. This is a documented Pacific connection in political ideas, not evidence that the two systems were identical.

The original parliament could debate taxation and public spending and make laws, while questions such as succession to the throne remained outside its authority. These distinctions show how representation developed within a monarchy.
Queen Salote contributed poetry and songs to Tongan cultural life. Her work used the Tongan language creatively, making the history of monarchy also a history of composition and performance.

Tongan migrants in New Zealand first held language-specific church gatherings in private homes and later established larger congregations. Since the 1980s, community preschools have helped children learn Tongan. These institutions support language through regular shared activity.

Czarina Wilson's Tonga-flag face mask, made in May 2020, entered Te Papa's collection. It records a designer applying her skills to a new public-health need. Contemporary objects like this keep the cultural story open beyond historical monuments and royal occasions.

ending.text: The British protectorate ended in 1970, and Tonga joined the Commonwealth that year. The kingdom continues. Its constitution, community institutions, language and artistic practices have changed across generations rather than ending at the map's last recorded snapshot.
